title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be, bound by law to do it. Illustrations. (a) A, a soldier, fires on a mob by the order of his superior officer, in conformity with the commands of the law. A has committed no offence. (b) A, an officer of a Court, being ordered by that Court to arrest Y, and, after due enquiry, believing Z to be Y, arrests Z. A has committed no offence.
plainMeaning: If the law requires you to do something, doing it is not an offence. The same protection applies if you honestly and carefully believed the law required it because you were mistaken about the facts — but not if you were mistaken about what the law says.
ingredients: The person was bound by law to do the act, or
believed he was bound by law because of a mistake of fact (not a mistake of law)
and that belief was held in good faith (with due care and attention)
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.76 IPC. Illustration (b) now says 'a Court' instead of 'a Court of Justice'; otherwise unchanged.

illustrations: A court orders a bailiff to seize a named person's car. The bailiff checks the registration papers carefully, but the papers were forged, and he seizes the wrong car. His mistake was about a fact, made in good faith, so he is protected.
A shopkeeper believes a new tax rule obliges him to detain customers who refuse to pay a surcharge. That is a mistake about the law, so s.14 does not protect him.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.14 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act of Judge when acting judicially
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law.
plainMeaning: A Judge is not guilty of an offence for what he does while acting judicially, if he uses a power the law gives him — or which he believes in good faith the law gives him.
ingredients: Done by a Judge
while acting judicially
in exercising a power that the law gives, or that he in good faith believes the law gives
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.77 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: A Magistrate sentences an accused to imprisonment, believing in good faith that he has power to do so. A higher court later finds the sentence exceeded his powers. The Magistrate has committed no offence (for example, of wrongful confinement).

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.15 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court
bareActText: Nothing which is done in pursuance of, or which is warranted by the judgment or order of, a Court; if done whilst such judgment or order remains in force, is an offence, notwithstanding the Court may have had no jurisdiction to pass such judgment or order, provided the person doing the act in good faith believes that the Court had such jurisdiction.
plainMeaning: A person who carries out a court's judgment or order, while it is still in force, commits no offence — even if the court turns out to have had no jurisdiction — provided he believed in good faith that the court did have jurisdiction.
ingredients: The act is done in pursuance of, or is warranted by, a court's judgment or order
The judgment or order is still in force when the act is done
The person believes in good faith that the court had jurisdiction
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.78 IPC. 'Court of Justice' is replaced by 'Court'; otherwise unchanged.

illustrations: A jail officer keeps a prisoner in custody under a court's warrant. The warrant is later set aside because the court lacked jurisdiction. The officer, who believed in good faith that the court had jurisdiction, committed no offence while the order was in force.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.16 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by any person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law, in doing it. Illustration. A sees Z commit what appears to A to be a murder. A, in the exercise, to the best of his judgment exerted in good faith, of the power which the law gives to all persons of apprehending murderers in the fact, seizes Z, in order to bring Z before the proper authorities. A has committed no offence, though it may turn out that Z was acting in self-defence.
plainMeaning: Where the law permits (justifies) an act, doing it is not an offence. The protection also covers someone who, because of a good-faith mistake of fact, believes the law justifies the act. The difference from s.14 is that s.14 is about acts the law requires, while s.17 is about acts the law allows.
ingredients: The person is justified by law in doing the act, or
believes he is justified by law because of a mistake of fact (not of law)
and holds that belief in good faith
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.79 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: At night, B sees a man breaking a neighbour's lock with a crowbar and holds him until the police arrive. It turns out the man owned the house and had lost his keys. B acted on a good-faith mistake of fact, so he is protected.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.17 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Accident in doing a lawful act
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by accident or misfortune, and without any criminal intention or knowledge in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means and with proper care and caution. Illustration. A is at work with a hatchet; the head flies off and kills a man who is standing by. Here, if there was no want of proper caution on the part of A, his act is excusable and not an offence.
plainMeaning: Harm caused purely by accident or misfortune is not an offence — but only if the person was doing something lawful, in a lawful way, by lawful means, with proper care and caution, and had no criminal intention or knowledge. Carelessness takes the act outside this exception.
ingredients: The harm was caused by accident or misfortune
No criminal intention or knowledge
The act was lawful, done in a lawful manner and by lawful means
Proper care and caution was taken
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.80 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: A driver keeping to the speed limit, with a properly serviced car, hits a child who suddenly runs out from behind a parked bus. If he took proper care, this is an accident within s.18.
A person practising target shooting in a crowded public park hits a passer-by. Firing where people are walking is not a lawful manner with proper care, so s.18 does not apply.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.18 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm
bareActText: Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property. Explanation.—It is a question of fact in such a case whether the harm to be prevented or avoided was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify or excuse the risk of doing the act with the knowledge that it was likely to cause harm. Illustrations. (a) A, the captain of a vessel, suddenly and without any fault or negligence on his part, finds himself in such a position that, before he can stop his vessel, he must inevitably run down a boat B, with twenty or thirty passengers on board, unless he changes the course of his vessel, and that, by changing his course, he must incur risk of running down a boat C with only two passengers on board, which he may possibly clear. Here, if A alters his course without any intention to run down the boat C and in good faith for the purpose of avoiding the danger to the passengers in the boat B, he is not guilty of an offence, though he may run down the boat C by doing an act which he knew was likely to cause that effect, if it be found as a matter of fact that the danger which he intended to avoid was such as to excuse him in incurring the risk of running down the boat C. (b) A, in a great fire, pulls down houses in order to prevent the conflagration from spreading. He does this with the intention in good faith of saving human life or property. Here, if it be found that the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to excuse A’s act, A is not guilty of the offence.
plainMeaning: This is the defence of necessity. Doing something you know is likely to cause harm is not an offence if you had no criminal intention to cause harm and acted in good faith to prevent or avoid other harm to a person or property. Whether the danger was serious and imminent enough to justify the risk is a question of fact.
ingredients: The act is done knowing it is likely to cause harm
There is no criminal intention to cause harm
It is done in good faith to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property
The harm avoided is of such a nature and so imminent as to justify the risk (a question of fact)
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.81 IPC. Illustration (a) now refers to 'a vessel' instead of 'a steam vessel'; otherwise unchanged.

illustrations: Floodwater is about to swamp a village. C breaks open a farmer's embankment to divert the water into an empty field, knowing the field will be damaged. If the danger to the village was serious and imminent, C commits no offence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.19 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act of a child under seven years of age
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
plainMeaning: A child under seven years of age cannot commit an offence. The protection is absolute: no enquiry into the child's understanding is needed.
ingredients: The person was a child under seven years of age when the act was done
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.82 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: A six-year-old picks up a phone left on a park bench and takes it home. Whatever the facts, the child has committed no offence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.20 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child above seven years of age and under twelve years of age, who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge of the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion.
plainMeaning: A child aged above seven and under twelve is not guilty of an offence if he had not yet developed enough maturity to understand the nature and consequences of what he did on that occasion. Unlike s.20, this protection depends on the child's actual maturity, judged for the particular act.
ingredients: The child was above seven and under twelve years of age
had not attained sufficient maturity of understanding
to judge the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.83 IPC. Now says 'under twelve years of age' (IPC: 'under twelve'); substance unchanged.

illustrations: A nine-year-old takes money from his mother's purse and, when questioned, lies and hides it carefully. The hiding suggests he understood that what he did was wrong, so the court may find he had sufficient maturity and s.21 may not protect him.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.21 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act of a person of unsound mind
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.
plainMeaning: A person is not guilty if, at the time of the act, unsoundness of mind made him incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it was wrong or against the law. What counts is his state of mind at the moment of the act, not before or after.
ingredients: Unsoundness of mind existed at the time of doing the act
Because of it, the person was incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or
incapable of knowing that it was wrong or contrary to law
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.84 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: During a psychotic episode, D attacks a neighbour believing him to be a demon about to kill his family. If he could not know the nature of his act or that it was wrong, s.22 applies.
E has a mental illness but plans a theft carefully and runs from the police. This suggests he knew the act was wrong, so s.22 may not apply.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.22 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law; provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
plainMeaning: Intoxication is a defence only if it was involuntary — the intoxicating thing was given to the person without his knowledge or against his will — and it made him incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or unlawful. Voluntary drunkenness is not a defence under this section.
ingredients: The person was intoxicated at the time of the act
The intoxicant was administered without his knowledge or against his will
Because of it, he was incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it was wrong or contrary to law
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.85 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: At a party, someone secretly mixes a strong drug into F's soft drink. In a confused state F damages a car. If he could not know what he was doing, s.23 protects him.
G chooses to drink heavily and then damages a car. His intoxication was voluntary, so s.23 does not apply.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.23 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated
bareActText: In cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
plainMeaning: Where an offence needs a particular knowledge or intent, a person who was voluntarily intoxicated is treated as having the same knowledge he would have had if sober. The law presumes knowledge, not intention. This does not apply if the intoxicant was given to him without his knowledge or against his will.
ingredients: The offence requires a particular knowledge or intent
The person did the act while intoxicated
He is treated as having the knowledge a sober person would have had
Unless the intoxicant was administered without his knowledge or against his will
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.86 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: H, drunk by choice, swings a heavy iron rod at a man's head. He is treated as knowing, as a sober person would, that such a blow is likely to cause death. Whether he had the intention to kill is still decided on the evidence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.24 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent
bareActText: Nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm. Illustration. A and Z agree to fence with each other for amusement. This agreement implies the consent of each to suffer any harm which, in the course of such fencing, may be caused without foul play; and if A, while playing fairly, hurts Z, A commits no offence.
plainMeaning: A person above eighteen can consent, expressly or impliedly, to suffer harm, or to take the risk of harm. Causing harm within that consent is not an offence, as long as the act was not intended, and not known to be likely, to cause death or grievous hurt. This covers contact sports and similar activities.
ingredients: The act is not intended, and not known to be likely, to cause death or grievous hurt
The person harmed is above eighteen years of age
He consented, expressly or impliedly, to suffer that harm or to take the risk of it
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.87 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: Two adult boxers fight a match under the rules. One breaks the other's nose with a fair punch. The loser consented to the risk of such harm, so there is no offence.
A boxer who deliberately hits his opponent after the referee has stopped the bout acts outside the consent, so s.25 does not protect him.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.25 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit
bareActText: Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm. Illustration. A, a surgeon, knowing that a particular operation is likely to cause the death of Z, who suffers under the painful complaint, but not intending to cause Z’s death, and intending, in good faith, Z’s benefit, performs that operation on Z, with Z’s consent. A has committed no offence.
plainMeaning: An act done in good faith for someone's benefit, with his consent, is not an offence because of the harm it causes, even if the doer knew it was likely to cause death, so long as he did not intend to cause death. This mainly protects doctors performing risky treatment with the patient's consent. There is no age limit in this section, but consent must be valid under s.28.
ingredients: Not intended to cause death
Done in good faith for the benefit of the person harmed
That person consented, expressly or impliedly, to suffer the harm or take the risk
Mere money benefit does not count as 'benefit' (Explanation to s.30)
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.88 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: A surgeon explains to an adult patient that a heart operation carries a high risk of death. The patient consents, the surgeon operates carefully in good faith, and the patient dies. The surgeon has committed no offence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.26 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent of guardian
bareActText: Nothing which is done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve years of age, or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent, either express or implied, of the guardian or other person having lawful charge of that person, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause or be known by the doer to be likely to cause to that person: Provided that this exception shall not extend to–– (a) the intentional causing of death, or to the attempting to cause death; (b) the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity; (c) the voluntary causing of grievous hurt, or to the attempting to cause grievous hurt, unless it be for the purpose of preventing death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity; (d) the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend. Illustration. A, in good faith, for his child’s benefit without his child’s consent, has his child cut for the stone by a surgeon knowing it to be likely that the operation will cause the child’s death, but not intending to cause the child’s death. A is within the exception, in as much as his object was the cure of the child.
plainMeaning: For a child under twelve or a person of unsound mind, the guardian (or person in lawful charge) can give consent. An act done in good faith for that person's benefit, by or with the guardian's consent, is not an offence because of the harm it causes. The proviso sets limits: it never covers intentionally causing (or attempting) death; it covers an act known to be likely to cause death only when done to prevent death or grievous hurt or to cure a grievous disease or infirmity; it covers voluntarily causing grievous hurt only for those same purposes; and it does not cover abetting an offence it would not cover.
ingredients: The person harmed is under twelve, or of unsound mind
The act is done in good faith for that person's benefit
It is done by, or with the express or implied consent of, the guardian or person in lawful charge
Not covered: intentionally causing (or attempting) death
Not covered: acts known likely to cause death, or grievous hurt, except to prevent death/grievous hurt or cure a grievous disease or infirmity
Not covered: abetment of an offence the exception would not cover
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.89 IPC. The four provisos are now lettered (a)-(d); substance unchanged.

illustrations: Parents consent to a risky operation to correct a serious heart defect in their four-year-old. The surgeon acts in good faith for the child's benefit. If the child is harmed, no offence is committed.
A guardian consents to a painful procedure on a ward of unsound mind purely to make him easier to manage, not for his benefit. The exception does not apply.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.27 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Consent known to be given under fear or misconception
bareActText: A consent is not such a consent as is intended by any section of this Sanhita,–– (a) if the consent is given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, and if the person doing the act knows, or has reason to believe, that the consent was given in consequence of such fear or misconception; or (b) if the consent is given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind, or intoxication, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives his consent; or (c) unless the contrary appears from the context, if the consent is given by a person who is under twelve years of age.
plainMeaning: This section says when apparent consent does not count. Consent is not valid if the doer knows, or has reason to believe, it was given out of fear of injury or a misconception of fact. It is also invalid if the person, because of unsoundness of mind or intoxication, could not understand what he was agreeing to. And, unless the context shows otherwise, consent by a child under twelve is not valid.
ingredients: (a) Consent given under fear of injury or a misconception of fact, which the doer knows or has reason to believe
(b) Consent by a person who, from unsoundness of mind or intoxication, cannot understand its nature and consequence
(c) Consent by a person under twelve, unless the contrary appears from the context
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.90 IPC. The three cases are now lettered (a)-(c); substance unchanged.

illustrations: J agrees to hand over his watch because K is holding a knife. K knows the 'consent' was given out of fear, so it is not valid consent.

A salesman gets an elderly customer to 'agree' to a treatment by falsely telling her it is free and harmless. Her consent rests on a misconception of fact that he knows about, so it is not valid consent.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.28 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Exclusion of acts which are offences independently of harm caused
bareActText: The exceptions in sections 25, 26 and 27 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or on whose behalf the consent is given. Illustration. Causing miscarriage (unless caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman) is an offence independently of any harm which it may cause or be intended to cause to the woman. Therefore, it is not an offence “by reason of such harm”; and the consent of the woman or of her guardian to the causing of such miscarriage does not justify the act.
plainMeaning: The consent exceptions in ss.25, 26 and 27 only answer offences that are offences because of the harm caused to the consenting person. They do not cover acts that are offences in themselves, whatever the harm, such as causing miscarriage (except in good faith to save the woman's life).
ingredients: Applies to the exceptions in ss.25, 26 and 27
They do not extend to acts that are offences independently of the harm caused to the consenting person
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.91 IPC. Now refers to ss.25, 26 and 27 (IPC ss.87, 88 and 89); substance unchanged.

illustrations: Two adults agree to fight a duel with swords in a public street. Even if both consent to the risk of injury, fighting in public disturbs the peace, which is an offence regardless of the harm to them, so consent does not help.

title: Act done in good faith for benefit of a person without consent
bareActText: Nothing is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause to a person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, even without that person’s consent, if the circumstances are such that it is impossible for that person to signify consent, or if that person is incapable of giving consent, and has no guardian or other person in lawful charge of him from whom it is possible to obtain consent in time for the thing to be done with benefit: Provided that this exception shall not extend to–– (a) the intentional causing of death, or the attempting to cause death; (b) the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity; (c) the voluntary causing of hurt, or to the attempting to cause hurt, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or hurt; (d) the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend. Illustrations. (1) Z is thrown from his horse, and is insensible. A, a surgeon, finds that Z requires to be trepanned. A, not intending Z’s death, but in good faith, for Z’s benefit, performs the trepan before Z recovers his power of judging for himself. A has committed no offence. (2) Z is carried off by a tiger. A fires at the tiger knowing it to be likely that the shot may kill Z, but not intending to kill Z, and in good faith intending Z’s benefit. A’s bullet gives Z a mortal wound. A has committed no offence. (3) A, a surgeon, sees a child suffer an accident which is likely to prove fatal unless an operation be immediately performed. There is no time to apply to the child’s guardian. A performs the operation in spite of the entreaties of the child, intending, in good faith, the child’s benefit. A has committed no offence. (4) A is in a house which is on fire, with Z, a child. People below hold out a blanket. A drops the child from the house top, knowing it to be likely that the fall may kill the child, but not intending to kill the child, and intending, in good faith, the child’s benefit. Here, even if the child is killed by the fall, A has committed no offence. Explanation.—Mere pecuniary benefit is not benefit within the meaning of sections 26, 27 and this section.
plainMeaning: In an emergency, an act done in good faith for someone's benefit is not an offence even without his consent, if he cannot signify consent (for example, he is unconscious) or is incapable of it, and no guardian can be reached in time. The proviso sets limits: it never covers intentionally causing (or attempting) death; an act known to be likely to cause death is covered only to prevent death or grievous hurt or to cure a grievous disease or infirmity; voluntarily causing hurt is covered only to prevent death or hurt; and it does not cover abetting an offence it would not cover. The Explanation adds that mere money benefit is not 'benefit' for ss.26, 27 and 30.
ingredients: Done in good faith for the person's benefit
Consent is impossible to signify, or the person is incapable of consenting
No guardian or person in lawful charge can be asked in time
Not covered: intentionally causing (or attempting) death
Not covered: acts known likely to cause death, except to prevent death/grievous hurt or cure a grievous disease
Not covered: causing hurt except to prevent death or hurt; or abetment of an offence not covered
Mere pecuniary benefit is not 'benefit'
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.92 IPC. Provisos lettered (a)-(d) and illustrations numbered (1)-(4); 'ball' becomes 'bullet'; the Explanation refers to ss.26, 27 and 30.

illustrations: An unconscious accident victim with no relatives present needs an emergency amputation to survive. A doctor operates in good faith without consent. No offence is committed.

A lifeguard drags a panicking swimmer out of the sea by the hair, causing some injury, to save him from drowning. The swimmer could not consent in the moment, and the act was for his benefit, so it is covered.

title: Communication made in good faith
bareActText: No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person. Illustration. A, a surgeon, in good faith, communicates to a patient his opinion that he cannot live. The patient dies in consequence of the shock. A has committed no offence, though he knew it to be likely that the communication might cause the patient’s death.
plainMeaning: Telling someone something in good faith for his own benefit is not an offence, even if the news harms him — for example, a doctor giving a patient a truthful but shocking diagnosis.
ingredients: A communication made in good faith
Made for the benefit of the person to whom it is made
Any harm to that person from the communication is not an offence
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.93 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: A doctor tells a patient, gently but honestly, that his cancer has spread. The patient suffers a heart attack from the shock. The doctor acted in good faith for the patient's benefit and committed no offence.

title: Act to which a person is compelled by threats
bareActText: Except murder, and offences against the State punishable with death, nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is compelled to do it by threats, which, at the time of doing it, reasonably cause the apprehension that instant death to that person will otherwise be the consequence: Provided that the person doing the act did not of his own accord, or from a reasonable apprehension of harm to himself short of instant death, place himself in the situation by which he became subject to such constraint. Explanation 1.—A person who, of his own accord, or by reason of a threat of being beaten, joins a gang of dacoits, knowing their character, is not entitled to the benefit of this exception, on the ground of his having been compelled by his associates to do anything that is an offence by law. Explanation 2.—A person seized by a gang of dacoits, and forced, by threat of instant death, to do a thing which is an offence by law; for example, a smith compelled to take his tools and to force the door of a house for the dacoits to enter and plunder it, is entitled to the benefit of this exception.
plainMeaning: This is the defence of duress. A person forced to do something by threats that reasonably make him fear instant death if he refuses is not guilty — except for murder and offences against the State punishable with death. He loses the defence if he put himself in that situation of his own accord, or out of fear of lesser harm, such as by voluntarily joining a gang of dacoits.
ingredients: Compelled to do the act by threats
The threats, at the time, reasonably cause fear of instant death to that person
Not available for murder, or offences against the State punishable with death
He did not place himself in that situation of his own accord, or from fear of harm short of instant death
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.94 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: Armed robbers seize a bank employee, put a gun to his head and force him to open the vault. He is protected by s.32 for opening it.
A man who voluntarily joins a criminal gang, knowing what it does, cannot later claim duress for crimes the gang pressures him into.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.32 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). title: Act causing slight harm
bareActText: Nothing is an offence by reason that it causes, or that it is intended to cause, or that it is known to be likely to cause, any harm, if that harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of such harm.
plainMeaning: The law does not punish trifles. An act is not an offence merely because it causes, or is intended or known to be likely to cause, harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of it.
ingredients: The act causes, or is intended or known to be likely to cause, harm
The harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.95 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: In a crowded metro, L brushes past M and lightly bumps his shoulder. The harm is so slight that no reasonable person would complain, so there is no offence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.33 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). title: Things done in private defence
bareActText: Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
plainMeaning: Anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence. Sections 35 to 44 then set out who may defend what, the limits, and how far the right goes.
ingredients: The act is done in the exercise of the right of private defence
The right must exist and be exercised within the limits in ss.35-44
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.96 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: N is attacked with a knife and pushes the attacker away, injuring him. If the conditions in ss.35-44 are met, N's act is not an offence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.34 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Right of private defence of body and of property
bareActText: Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 37, to defend— (a) his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body; (b) the property, whether movable or immovable, of himself or of any other person, against any act which is an offence falling under the definition of theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or which is an attempt to commit theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass.
plainMeaning: Everyone may defend his own body and anyone else's against any offence affecting the human body. He may also defend his own or anyone else's property, movable or immovable, against theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or an attempt at them. The right is subject to the restrictions in s.37.
ingredients: Body: one's own or any other person's, against any offence affecting the human body
Property: one's own or anyone else's, movable or immovable
Property is defended only against theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or attempts at these
Subject to the restrictions in s.37
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.97 IPC. Now refers to the restrictions in s.37 (IPC s.99); substance unchanged.

illustrations: P sees a stranger being beaten in the street and steps in to stop the attack. He is exercising the right of private defence of another person's body.
Q sees someone trying to steal his neighbour's scooter and grabs the thief. He is defending another person's property against theft.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.35 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Right of private defence against act of a person of unsound mind, etc.
bareActText: When an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence. Illustrations. (a) Z, a person of unsound mind, attempts to kill A; Z is guilty of no offence. But A has the same right of private defence which he would have if Z were sane. (b) A enters by night a house which he is legally entitled to enter. Z, in good faith, taking A for a house-breaker, attacks A. Here Z, by attacking A under this misconception, commits no offence. But A has the same right of private defence against Z, which he would have if Z were not acting under that misconception.
plainMeaning: The right of private defence exists even against someone who cannot be guilty of an offence because of youth, immaturity, unsoundness of mind, intoxication or a misconception. You may defend yourself as if the act were an offence.
ingredients: The act would otherwise be an offence
It is not an offence because of the doer's youth, immaturity, unsoundness of mind, intoxication or misconception
The defender has the same right of private defence as if it were an offence
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.98 IPC. Illustration (a) says 'a person of unsound mind' instead of 'under the influence of madness'; substance unchanged.

illustrations: A ten-year-old swings a heavy iron rod at R's head. Even if the child might not be guilty of an offence, R may defend himself as he could against an adult.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.36 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Acts against which there is no right of private defence
bareActText: (1) There is no right of private defence,–– (a) against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done, by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that act, may not be strictly justifiable by law; (b) against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or of grievous hurt, if done, or attempted to be done, by the direction of a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though that direction may not be strictly justifiable by law; (c) in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. (2) The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence. Explanation 1.—A person is not deprived of the right of private defence against an act done, or attempted to be done, by a public servant, as such, unless he knows or has reason to believe, that the person doing the act is such public servant. Explanation 2.—A person is not deprived of the right of private defence against an act done, or attempted to be done, by the direction of a public servant, unless he knows, or has reason to believe, that the person doing the act is acting by such direction, or unless such person states the authority under which he acts, or if he has authority in writing, unless he produces such authority, if demanded.
plainMeaning: The right of private defence has limits. It does not exist against a public servant (or someone acting on his direction) acting in good faith under colour of his office, unless the act reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt — even if the act is not strictly lawful. It does not exist where there is time to seek the protection of the public authorities. And it never allows more harm than is necessary for defence. You lose the right against a public servant only if you knew, or had reason to believe, he was one.
ingredients: (1)(a) No right against a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office, unless the act reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt
(1)(b) Same for a person acting by the direction of such a public servant
(1)(c) No right where there is time to seek protection from the public authorities
(2) Never more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence
Explanations: the right is lost only if the defender knows or has reason to believe the doer is a public servant (or is acting on his direction)
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.99 IPC. Restrictions arranged as sub-sections (1)(a)-(c) and (2); the same two Explanations; substance unchanged.

illustrations: A police officer, acting in good faith, arrests S under a warrant that later turns out to be defective. The arrest does not threaten death or grievous hurt, so S has no right to resist with force.

T is slapped once by a man who then stands in front of him shouting. T responds by stabbing him in the chest. A slap does not justify anything like that much harm, so s.37(2) takes the stabbing outside private defence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.37 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: When right of private defence of body extends to causing death
bareActText: The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:— (a) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (b) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (c) an assault with the intention of committing rape; (d) an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; (e) an assault with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; (f) an assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release; (g) an act of throwing or administering acid or an attempt to throw or administer acid which may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.
plainMeaning: Defending the body may go as far as intentionally causing death, but only against the serious assaults listed: one reasonably feared to cause death; one reasonably feared to cause grievous hurt; an assault intending rape, or to gratify unnatural lust; one intending kidnapping or abduction; one intending wrongful confinement where the victim reasonably fears he cannot reach the authorities; and throwing or administering acid (or attempting it) where grievous hurt is reasonably feared. The limits in s.37 still apply.
ingredients: Subject to the restrictions in s.37
(a) assault reasonably causing fear of death
(b) assault reasonably causing fear of grievous hurt
(c) assault with intent to commit rape
(d) assault with intent to gratify unnatural lust
(e) assault with intent to kidnap or abduct
(f) assault with intent to wrongfully confine, where the victim reasonably fears he cannot seek help from the authorities
(g) throwing or administering acid, or attempting it, reasonably causing fear of grievous hurt
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.100 IPC. Refers to 'the restrictions specified in section 37' instead of 'the last preceding section'; the seven cases (including acid attack, added to the IPC in 2013) are lettered (a)-(g).

illustrations: At night on a lonely road, a man carrying a bottle of acid tries to throw it at U's face. U strikes him with a rod and he dies. U's act can fall within s.38(g).
V is pushed during a minor argument. A push does not reasonably cause fear of death or grievous hurt, so s.38 does not allow V to cause death.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.38 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: When such right extends to causing any harm other than death
bareActText: If the offence be not of any of the descriptions specified in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death.
plainMeaning: If the attack on the body is not one of the serious kinds listed in s.38, the defender may cause any harm other than death, still within the limits in s.37.
ingredients: The offence is not of a kind listed in s.38
The right does not extend to voluntarily causing death
It does extend to causing any other harm, subject to s.37
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.101 IPC. Refers to s.38 and s.37 by number instead of 'the last preceding section' and s.99; substance unchanged.

illustrations: W is punched in the face during a fight that does not threaten death or grievous hurt. He may hit back to defend himself, but not so as to kill.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.39 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body
bareActText: The right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence though the offence may not have been committed; and it continues as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues.
plainMeaning: The right to defend the body starts as soon as there is a reasonable fear of danger to the body from an attempt or threat to commit the offence — you need not wait to be hit. It lasts as long as that reasonable fear continues.
ingredients: Starts as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises
from an attempt or threat to commit the offence, even if the offence has not yet been committed
Continues as long as that apprehension of danger continues
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.102 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: X raises a knife and advances towards Y shouting that he will stab him. Y's right of private defence begins at once; he need not wait until he is stabbed.
After Y knocks the knife away, X runs off. The danger has ended, so Y may not chase X and beat him.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.40 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: When right of private defence of property extends to causing death
bareActText: The right of private defence of property extends, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which, occasions the exercise of the right, be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:— (a) robbery; (b) house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise; (c) mischief by fire or any explosive substance committed on any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling, or as a place for the custody of property; (d) theft, mischief, or house-trespass, under such circumstances as may reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence, if such right of private defence is not exercised.
plainMeaning: Defending property may go as far as causing death only against: robbery; house-breaking between sunset and sunrise; mischief by fire or explosives on a building, tent or vessel used as a dwelling or for keeping property; and theft, mischief or house-trespass where death or grievous hurt is reasonably feared if the right is not used. The limits in s.37 still apply.
ingredients: Subject to the restrictions in s.37
(a) robbery
(b) house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise
(c) mischief by fire or explosive on a building, tent or vessel used as a dwelling or to keep property
(d) theft, mischief or house-trespass that reasonably causes fear of death or grievous hurt if the right is not exercised
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.103 IPC. 'House-breaking by night' becomes 'house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise'; clause (c) now covers mischief by fire 'or any explosive substance'.

illustrations: At 2 a.m., intruders break into Z's house through a window. Z may, if necessary, use force up to causing death, because this is house-breaking between sunset and sunrise.
In daylight, a man picks a ripe mango from Z's tree and walks off. Z may not cause his death to protect the fruit.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.41 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: When such right extends to causing any harm other than death
bareActText: If the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which occasions the exercise of the right of private defence, be theft, mischief, or criminal trespass, not of any of the descriptions specified in section 41, that right does not extend to the voluntary causing of death, but does extend, subject to the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the wrong-doer of any harm other than death.
plainMeaning: Against theft, mischief or criminal trespass that is not one of the serious kinds in s.41, the defender of property may cause any harm other than death, within the limits in s.37.
ingredients: The offence is theft, mischief or criminal trespass, not of a kind in s.41
The right does not extend to voluntarily causing death
It does extend to causing any other harm, subject to s.37
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.104 IPC. Refers to s.41 and s.37 by number; substance unchanged.

illustrations: AA finds a youth spray-painting his shop shutter in the afternoon and pushes him away, causing a bruise. That is within the right; killing him would not be.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.42 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023). IPC correspondence and change note checked against the text of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (government-hosted consolidated copy, Maharashtra Police) read with the amending Acts of 2000 (IT Act, First Schedule), 2005 (Acts 2 and 25 of 2005), 2013 (Act 13 of 2013) and 2018 (Act 22 of 2018).

title: Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of property
bareActText: The right of private defence of property,–– (a) commences when a reasonable apprehension of danger to the property commences; (b) against theft continues till the offender has effected his retreat with the property or either the assistance of the public authorities is obtained, or the property has been recovered; (c) against robbery continues as long as the offender causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint or as long as the fear of instant death or of instant hurt or of instant personal restraint continues; (d) against criminal trespass or mischief continues as long as the offender continues in the commission of criminal trespass or mischief; (e) against house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise continues as long as the house-trespass which has been begun by such house-breaking continues.
plainMeaning: The right to defend property starts when there is a reasonable fear of danger to the property. How long it lasts depends on the offence: against theft, until the thief has got away with the property, help from the public authorities is obtained, or the property is recovered; against robbery, as long as the robber causes or attempts death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or the fear of instant death, hurt or restraint lasts; against criminal trespass or mischief, as long as the offender continues it; and against night-time house-breaking, as long as the house-trespass it began continues.
ingredients: (a) Starts when a reasonable apprehension of danger to property begins
(b) Theft: until the offender has retreated with the property, public help is obtained, or the property is recovered
(c) Robbery: while death, hurt or wrongful restraint is caused or attempted, or fear of instant death, hurt or restraint lasts
(d) Criminal trespass or mischief: while the offender continues it
(e) House-breaking between sunset and sunrise: while the house-trespass it began continues
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.105 IPC. Arranged as clauses (a)-(e); 'house-breaking by night' becomes 'house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise'.

illustrations: BB chases a thief who has just snatched her bag and catches him two streets away, before he has escaped. The right of private defence against theft still continues, and she may use reasonable force to recover the bag.
A week later BB recognises the thief in a market. The theft is long over, so she has no right of private defence; she should go to the police.

title: Right of private defence against deadly assault when there is risk of harm to innocent person
bareActText: If in the exercise of the right of private defence against an assault which reasonably causes the apprehension of death, the defender be so situated that he cannot effectually exercise that right without risk of harm to an innocent person, his right of private defence extends to the running of that risk. Illustration. A is attacked by a mob who attempt to murder him. He cannot effectually exercise his right of private defence without firing on the mob, and he cannot fire without risk of harming young children who are mingled with the mob. A commits no offence if by so firing he harms any of the children.
plainMeaning: If a person facing an assault that reasonably causes fear of death cannot defend himself effectively without risking harm to an innocent person, his right of private defence extends to taking that risk.
ingredients: An assault that reasonably causes apprehension of death
The defender cannot effectively defend himself without risk of harm to an innocent person
The right of private defence extends to running that risk
punishment: Not applicable — this is a general exception (a defence), not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.106 IPC. Wording retained.

illustrations: Armed attackers surround CC's car and try to kill him. He drives off at speed to escape and, in doing so, hits a bystander. His right of private defence extended to running that risk.
